node.label: Patricia Hill Collins
node.date_label: “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986) · Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) · Fighting Words (1998) · Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019)
node.description: Collins argues that Black women's ideas and actions are central to social justice, not marginal, and that Black women produce critical social theory outside elite institutions. Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) develops this argument: it sets out a Black feminist standpoint epistemology, analyses the “controlling images” through which Black women are represented, and describes intersecting oppressions as a “matrix of domination”; she later described it as examining Black feminist thought “as an example of critical social theory that did not come from elites.” Her earlier article “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986) set out the sociological significance of Black feminist thought. In “Truth-Telling and Intellectual Activism” (2013) she discusses speaking to several audiences at once. “Intersectionality’s Definitional Dilemmas” (2015) treats intersectionality as a knowledge project attentive to power relations, and Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019) asks how critical analysis and social action might inform one another.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Learning from the Outsider Within” (1986); Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised second edition 2000); Fighting Words (1998); Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019).
node.scope_note: The 1986 article, the 2000 book and Higginbotham's 1992 essay were not read on a permitted route; the 2015 and 2013 articles are known from their abstracts; selected 2024 interview responses; and parts of the publisher’s 2019 introduction were read. The original 1990 book, complete monographs, and cited originals by hooks, Kuhn, Crenshaw, Hall, Said and Du Bois were not read. Fighting Words is identified bibliographically only.

people_update.label: Patricia Hill Collins
people_update.identity_note: Collins describes herself as having grown up “a Black girl from a working-class family” (interview, Revista Brasileira de Educação, 2024).

proposed_edges.relationship: In her published education interview (2024), Collins credits Du Bois’s historical and sociological scholarship with sharpening her approach to critical education.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: First response, Harvard-training paragraph: “sharpened my critical education toolkit.” Specific Du Bois work and date unidentified; original scholarship unread here. This is retrospective testimony, not a teacher–student relationship.

proposed_edges.relationship: Black Feminist Thought (1990; revised 2000) treats Black women's thought, developed outside elite institutions and in Black women's own communities and political work, as critical social theory, as Collins describes it in 2019 and in a 2024 interview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). Duke University Press's own preview of the 2019 book (introduction p. 3) and the open SciELO interview (Collins: 'Black Feminist Thought presents numerous examples of how education constitutes a site of Black women's political engagement'; 'I examine how Black women have developed a series of safe spaces that enabled Black feminist thought to flourish') support a narrower contribution. Replace the source_ids with phcw_theory_2019 and phcw_interview_2024. Phrase seen: “in previous work, I examined Black feminist thought as an example of critical social theory that did not come from elites (Collins 1998a; 2000)” Read at: https://assets-us-01.kc-usercontent.com/f7ca9afb-82c2-002a-a423-84e111d5b498/f0698fc2-2ecb-46cb-8cc8-335f7535c0bb/978-1-4780-0646-6_601.pdf
proposed_edges.map_label: Black women's thought as social theory

proposed_edges.relationship: In a 2019 interview about Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), published in Tempo Social in 2021, Collins says that Smith’s framework for decolonizing methodology (Decolonizing Methodologies, 1999) develops the kind of intellectual and political praxis that intersectionality needs.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete English interview PDF on Tempo Social’s own site (Tempo Social 33:1, 2021, pp. 323–355; interview held at USP on 29 October 2019). On p. 333, ending her answer to Marcos Nobre on methodology and praxis, Collins says: “Linda Tuhiwai Smith’s framework for decolonizing methodology develops the kind of intellectual and political praxis needed for intersectionality (Smith, 1999)”. The reference list (p. 354) gives Decolonizing Methodologies (Zed, 1999). This is an explicit, named intellectual resource stated by Collins, not an acknowledgment list. Smith’s name also appears among people thanked in the 2019 acknowledgments (Duke preview, p. x), which is not counted. Unread: the corresponding passage in the 2019 book. OCAP: the edge concerns Smith’s published research methodology only; it states no community knowledge or identity.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins places Beauvoir’s analyses of oppression and freedom in dialogue with Pauli Murray’s, arguing that Beauvoir, though familiar with oppressions of race, gender, class and sexuality, never advanced an intersectional analysis; in a 2019 interview she describes this as engaging Beauvoir’s ideas rather than criticizing her.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Two permitted readings. (1) Duke University Press’s own preview of the 2019 book, introduction pp. 13–14, chapter summary beginning “In Chapter 6, ‘Intersectionality and the Question of Freedom’”: “Placing the ideas of two feminist intellectuals in dialogue”, and “despite being familiar with oppressions of race, gender, class, and sexuality, Beauvoir never advanced an intersectional analysis of oppression or freedom”. (2) Tempo Social interview (2021), pp. 337–338: Collins says she gives “a close reading of the work of Simone de Beauvoir” (The Ethics of Ambiguity, 1947; The Second Sex, 1949), juxtaposes it with Pauli Murray, and that “My goal was not to criticize Beauvoir to make room for my own arguments, but rather to engage her ideas as a way of pushing my own.” The chapter body is unread, so the claim is limited to Collins’s own summaries. The chapter number differs: 6 in the book’s introduction, 5 in the interview; the edge follows the book. Typed as a comparison because Collins herself disclaims a critique. Same pair as held beauvoir_w_06 (Beauvoir packet: Collins’s 2017 chapter, publisher summary only): this edge rests on a different work and a different route.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins develops intersectionality as a critical social theory in the making, distinguishing its core concepts from its guiding principles and mapping the field through how people use it; the book follows her earlier mapping of the field with Margaret Andersen in Race, Class, and Gender.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke University Press preview, introduction p. 9 (“As a critical social theory in the making, intersectionality has a stake in clarifying what being critical means for its own project”, read on pp. 8–9) and pp. 17–18 (through nine editions of Race, Class, and Gender, “Margaret Andersen and I … effectively mapping the field every three years”). Tempo Social interview (2021), p. 332: “I chose to map the field by examining how people used intersectionality” and “in chapter 1, I finally was able to distinguish intersectionality’s core concepts from its guiding principles”. Supplementary: Keisha Jefferies’s review of Collins and Bilge, Intersectionality (2nd ed., 2020), Atlantis 41.2 (2020), p. 100, praises its “informative and fulsome discussion of the genealogy of intersectionality”. Limits: book chapters unread beyond the introduction. The edge makes no claim that Collins originated the term; Crenshaw’s term and the earlier Black feminist roots stay as the existing node describes them.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins examines the critical theory of the Frankfurt school, with British cultural studies and Francophone social theory, as a site of critical social theory against which she clarifies intersectionality’s own critical project; in 2019 she said the Frankfurt School “rightfully claims the term ‘Critical Theory’”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke preview, introduction p. 9, summary of chapter 2, “What’s Critical about Critical Social Theory?”: “I examine three particular sites of critical social theory … critical theory of the Frankfurt school (1930s–1940s), British cultural studies (1970s–1980s), and strands of Francophone social theory (1950s–1960s)”. Tempo Social interview (2021), p. 331, answering Marcos Nobre’s question on the Frankfurt School: “the Frankfurt School rightfully claims the term ‘Critical Theory’ and does incorporate praxis into their framework … My selection of critical theories was deliberate.” Chapter 2 itself is unread; the claim is limited to Collins’s own summaries. No claim of membership in or debt to the School. British cultural studies is named in the same sentence but is not proposed as a separate edge (see edge_search_log).

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Theorising power and resistance under contemporary capitalism” (2024), Fraser describes Collins’s Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019) as a critical theoretical account and relates Collins’s aim of explaining how gender, race and class co-constitute one another to her own analysis of these divisions within capitalist society.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the open interview on the journal publisher’s own site. In the answer to Charles Masquelier’s question about the post-intersectional subtitle of her first Benjamin Lecture, Fraser explicitly appraises Collins’s account as critical theoretical. In the seventh paragraph of that answer she connects her own effort to explain gender, race and class within capitalist society with Collins’s aim of explaining their co-constitution. The question and the following interviewer turn identify the 2019 book; the reference list abbreviates its title. This is substantive named engagement, not a shared-topic inference. Classified as an undirected comparison: Fraser’s subsequent reservation about the depth of explanation in existing intersectionality theory is general, so it is not represented as a criticism specifically of Collins. No claim about Collins’s response to Fraser or about influence in the other direction. Collins’s book and Fraser’s Benjamin Lectures were not read in this pass.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Feminist Army” (2016), Sara Ahmed draws on Collins’s Black Feminist Thought (1990; citing the revised 2000 edition) to examine how Sojourner Truth challenges racial exclusions in the category of woman, while acknowledging the mediation of the surviving speech account.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ahmed engages Collins’s interpretation in the essay’s body, with citations to pages 12–13. This supports a specific interpretive resource, not a general intellectual genealogy. Collins’s book was not read for this task.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses Collins’s reading of Sojourner Truth

row.context: Treats Black women’s everyday intellectual production as knowledge and questions its exclusion from scholarship; a theoretical contribution with contested standpoint claims.
Sociologist who develops intersectionality as a critical social theory in the making and maps how the field uses it.
row.works: Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019); with Sirma Bilge, Intersectionality (2016; 2nd ed. 2020).
